paper_title: HERIT: Enabling Global Access to Hanja-to-English Historical Translation by Mitigating Temporal Bias

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Historical archives are invaluable for multidisciplinary research but remain inaccessible globally due to severe language barriers. While manual translation is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, simply applying existing machine translation models is inadequate due to unique linguistic nuances and the temporal bias inherent in scarce human-labeled corpora. To address these challenges, we propose HERIT, a systematic domain-adaptation pipeline that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to generate high-quality pseudo-labeled data from abundant Hanja-Korean corpora. This approach substantially expands the training dataset, mitigating both data scarcity and temporal overfitting across different historical periods. Extensive automated and human evaluations demonstrate that HERIT consistently outperforms baselines. Finally, we translate previously untranslated portions of the archives using our model, thereby enabling global access to these resources for researchers.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Historical archives are invaluable for multidisciplinary research but remain inaccessible globally due to severe language barriers. While manual translation is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, simply applying existing machine translation models is inadequate due to unique linguistic nuances and the temporal bias inherent in scarce human-labeled corpora. To address these challenges, we propose HERIT, systematic domain-adaptation pipeline that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to generate high-quality pseudolabeled data from abundant Hanja-Korean corpora. This approach substantially expands the training dataset, mitigating both data scarcity and temporal overfitting across different historical periods. Extensive automated and human evaluations demonstrate that HERIT consistently outperforms baselines. Finally, we translate previously untranslated portions of the archives using our model, thereby enabling global access to these resources for researchers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Historical records have been vital source for discovering knowledge and deriving insights. In the humanities, these archives allow researchers to analyze political dynamics and cultural evolution. In the natural sciences, they serve as crucial sources for tracking natural phenomena, such as solar eclipses, supernovae, and seismic activities. The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (AJD) and the Journal of the Royal Secretariat (JRS) are regarded as preeminent historical archives, recognized not only in Korea but globally. They provide comprehensive records spanning over 500 years, comprising vast array of subjects. Extending beyond state affairs and administration, they meticulously chronicle natural phenomena, including astronomical observations, seismic activity, famines, and epidemics. Accordingly, researchers worldwide utilize these archives across broad spectrum of disciplines, from the social to the natural sciences. Given their significance, the translation of the AJD from Hanja into Korean has been completed, while the translation of the JRS is currently underway. Furthermore, to promote the global accessibility of these historical archives, the National Institute of Korean History (NIKH) launched project to translate the AJD into English. However, relying on manual translation by experts proficient in both Hanja and English presents significant challenges; the project is projected to span 22 years with budget of approximately 20 million USD.1 Furthermore, applying this manual approach to other archives such as the JRS, which is five times more voluminous than the AJD, would require prohibitive costs in both time and resources. Consequently, existing human-translated English corpora are not only scarce but also heavily skewed towards specific reigns. Improving translation on unseen historical periods requires method that generalizes beyond this temporal bias. Since these archives are written in Hanja, leveraging Chinese-English LLMs appears to be an intuitive solution for processing these corpora. However, such an approach encounters significant challenges. First, there is fundamental script mismatch: Chinese models typically utilize Simplified Chinese, whereas Korean Hanja retains Traditional Chinese forms, resulting in character incompatibility. Second, substantial semantic and syntactic discrepancies exist. Even when characters are identical, semantic divergence is common, as homographs have often evolved distinct meanings in the respective languages. Furthermore, the texts contain Korea-specific Hanja usage that reflects native grammatical structures, and the word order 1https://sillok.history.go.kr/eslk/about/tran *Corresponding author slationProjectInfo.do frequently deviates from standard Chinese syntax. Most critically, Chinese-English models transliterate proper nouns, such as personal names and geographical locations, based on Chinese pronunciation rather than Korean pronunciation. This misalignment not only degrades translation quality but also introduces factual errors. To address these challenges, we propose systematic domain-adaptation pipeline for training Hanja-to-English model specialized for historical archives, harnessing human-translated corpora, as shown in Fig. 1. To overcome the scarcity and temporal overfitting of available expert data, we introduce retrieval-augmented in-context learning for data augmentation strategy that generates highquality pseudo-labeled data. This effectively alleviates data sparsity while minimizing overfitting to specific eras. Subsequently, we present HERIT: Hanja-English RAG-based Intelligent Translation model for historical archives. Extensive evaluations, including quantitative metrics and human expert assessments, demonstrate that HERIT significantly outperforms existing baselines. In addition, we translate the remaining untranslated portions of the JRS and AJD using our model. Our model and the translated corpus are publicly available2 to facilitate future research.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Historical archives have extensively contributed to diverse research domains. In the field of social sciences, they provide foundational data for analyzing international affairs (Thies, 2002), demography (Alter, 2019), economic conditions (Clark, 2007), and linguistic transitions (Wei et al., 2025). In parallel, the natural sciences leverage historical records to investigate natural phenomena such as astronomical events (Wang et al., 2021; Wei and Yan, 2024) and climate change (Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). Thus, historical documents serve as invaluable resources across diverse fields, offering lens through which to understand past events and derive critical insights for both the present and the future. Korean archives, such as AJD and JRS, are recognized as invaluable resources by the global academic community for their comprehensive scope, spanning multiple centuries and covering wide array of subjects. Notably, the continuous and systematic management of these records makes them par2https://github.com/dandamdandam/HERIT ticularly advantageous for analyzing macroscopic changes. For instance, they have been extensively utilized in studies concerning astronomical observations and geological phenomena, as well as disasters such as epidemics, and even economic crises (Stephenson, 2011; Yang et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021; Wei and Yan, 2024; Rhee, 2014; Hwang, 2022). With advances in machine learning, such as OCR and machine translation, research has been conducted to effectively translate historical archives into modern languages. Afli and Way (2016) proposed method to digitize historical documents written in 17th-century French using OCR and translate them into Modern English by applying stochastic machine translation techniques. To translate Ancient Chinese into Modern Chinese, Zhang et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2019) developed passagelevel alignment methods and deep neural networkbased machine translation models. Among Korean historical documents, the AJD has been fully translated into Korean by the NIKH, whereas the translation of the JRS remains ongoing due to its vast volume. Addressing this, Kang et al. (2021) developed Hanja-to-Korean translation model leveraging the parallel corpus derived from both the AJD and JRS. Concurrently, project to translate the original Hanja text of the AJD into English is underway, with the records from the era of King Sejong (approximately 2.5% of the total) currently completed. Using this partial Hanja-English corpus alongside the Hanja-Korean data, Son et al. (2022) proposed Hanja-Korean-English multilingual model. However, due to the scarcity of humantranslated Hanja-English data, the performance of models trained from scratch remains limited. Recent LLMs, such as Gemini-2.5 (Comanici et al., 2025), Sonnet-4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), KimiK2 (Team et al., 2025), GPT-5.1 (OpenAI, 2025), and Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning capabilities. This advancement enables them to utilize information during the inference phase via few-shot learning, even without having encountered it during the pretraining or fine-tuning stages (Brown et al., 2020). Specifically, RAG further improves performance by incorporating retrieved examples relevant to the input into the prompt (Lewis et al., 2020). Consequently, there is active research into data augmentation approaches for data-scarce domains that leverage these few-shot learning and RAG strategies (Seo et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024). Moreover, Hanja Korean English 疫疾 世宗 江原道 강원도 Kangwon Province Epidemic disease King Sejong 역질 세종 Table 1: Examples of glossary information: Hanja source, Korean pronunciation, and English translation. methods such as Best-of-N (BoN) (Liu et al., 2024) and Fusion-of-N (FusioN) (Khairi et al., 2025) have been proposed to further enhance performance by generating multiple candidate responses and aggregating them to derive final answer. We address the scarcity of historical parallel corpora by leveraging RAG-based augmentation. Specifically, we construct high-quality pseudolabeled dataset using Hanja-Korean corpora via retrieval-augmented in-context learning and FusioN. Finally, we fine-tune pre-trained LLM, leveraging its inherent English proficiency and partial Hanja understanding.

sections.title: 3 Datasets
sections.content: As noted in Section 2, the translation of the AJD is ongoing; currently, only the Annals of King Sejong have been fully translated. For our experiments, we obtained the AJD documents from NIKH3. Using these human-translated documents, we compiled corpus yielding 350K Hanja-Korean pairs and 17.7K Hanja-Korean-English triples4. From the Hanja-English subset, we allocated 1,000 records each to the validation set Dvalid and the test set Dtest, with the remaining 15.7K samples constituting the training set Dtrain. To mitigate periodspecific evaluation bias, we constructed an additional test set for human evaluation, Dtest NT , by sampling 80 records per king (2,080 entries total) from the untranslated corpus. Crucially, Dtest NT was strictly excluded from both the pseudo-labeling process and the training data. To prevent data leakage, we implemented rigorous decontamination pipeline. Given that Hanja is an ideographic script where individual characters carry dense semantic information, characterlevel exact and edit-based matching is particularly effective. Specifically, for each test instance, we retrieved the top-10 candidate matches from Dtrain 3https://www.history.go.kr/en/main/main.do 4Since all AJD documents were originally translated from Hanja to Korean, the Hanja-English data naturally forms (Hanja, Korean, English) triples. using BM25 and computed their character-level normalized Levenshtein similarity. We discarded any candidate exceeding similarity threshold of 0.9. We chose this threshold because historical archives frequently feature formalized administrative templates where changing single entity or action drastically alters the translation semantics; lowering the threshold below 0.9 would excessively discard valid, semantically distinct evaluation instances. This pipeline filtered out 83 samples from Dtest, 3 from Dtest NT , and 1 from the 200-sample human evaluation subset, leaving the evaluation splits well-isolated from Dtrain. Detailed examples and similarity distribution for the deduplication process are provided in Appendix A. Using Dtrain as an external knowledge base, we applied retrieval-augmented in-context learning for pseudo-labeling to the untranslated corpus (details in Section 4.2). After filtering out documents longer than 800 characters, we constructed an augmented dataset, Daug, comprising 315K pseudo-labeled samples from all reigns except King Sejongs. Finally, both Dtrain and Daug were utilized to train our model. In addition, NIKH provides lexical resources, including semantic meanings and English pronunciations of proper nouns (e.g., personal and geographical names). Leveraging this data enables the LLM to comprehend Hanja documents more effectively and accurately translate proper nouns into English based on their correct pronunciation. Consequently, we compiled glossary consisting of 25K entries from these lexicons and utilized it during the pseudo-labeling process.

sections.title: 4 Proposed Methods
sections.content: This section presents our method for enhancing pseudo-label quality, followed by an introduction to our model fine-tuned on blend of pseudo-labeled and expert-translated datasets.

sections.title: 4.1 Selecting the Backbone LLM for
sections.content: Pseudo-Labeling Since the pseudo-labeling process can incur substantial API costs due to the large volume of target historical documents, evaluating candidate LLMs in terms of both performance and costeffectiveness is essential for selecting the optimal backbone. To this end, we first assessed the translation performance of various LLMs on Dtest using base prompts. We employed standard metrics Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework for translating historical documents into English. The framework comprises three main stages: 1) pseudo-labeling for data augmentation, 2) fine-tuning the LLM by integrating human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data, and 3) translation of the untranslated corpus using the trained model. for machine translation, including BLEU (Post, 2018), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and chrF++ (Popovic, 2017). As shown in Table 2, Hunyuan-MT-7B, despite being leading Chinese translation model (Zheng et al., 2025), underperforms on Hanja translation. This result underscores the need for models specifically designed for Hanja. Results from the Qwen3 families demonstrate that translation quality generally improves as underlying model size increases. Regarding reasoning capabilities, while Gemini2.5-Flash shows performance gains, Sonnet-4.5 experiences slight decline. This aligns with prior surveys suggesting that reasoning does not significantly contribute to machine translation performance (Zebaze et al., 2025). similar trend is observed with Gemini-2.5-Pro as shown in Table 4. Although Gemini-2.5-Pro achieves the highest accuracy, it incurs higher inference costs due to its size and reasoning overhead. In contrast, Gemini2.5-Flash offers the most cost-effective trade-off, achieving competitive performance at fraction of the cost. Therefore, we adopt Gemini-2.5-Flash for the pseudo-labeling process.

(R) denotes the integration of reasoning capabilities. in Step 1-1, the Proposer takes untranslated source documents to generate multiple translation drafts. In Step 1-2, the Fusor takes these drafts along with the original source document to generate the final translation. Since this architecture generates the final sentence by ensembling the Proposers drafts in the Fusor, it not only mitigates mistranslation but also enhances translation quality by leveraging expanded information through holistic examination of the drafts. As depicted in Fig. 1, our goal is to improve the pseudo-label quality of the Proposer and Fusor by enriching the input prompt with auxiliary information, instead of relying solely on the Hanja document. To address the limited proficiency of LLMs in understanding Hanja, we augment the input with the corresponding Korean text to enhance contextual understanding. To ensure the accurate translation of proper nouns, we utilize curated glossary by appending terms to the prompt when exact matches are found in the source text. We additionally utilize few-shot prompting to capture the nuances, including contextual and lexical information, of Hanja-to-English translation. Specifically, we adopt RAG that retrieves the top-K similar documents S(h) from Dtrain for given input Hanja document via an embedding-based retriever. These retrieved entries are fed into both the Proposer and the Fusor as few-shot demonstrations in the form of (Hanja, Korean, English) triples. We optimized the hyperparameters for pseudolabeling based on the experiments described in Section 5.1. To balance performance and inference cost, we selected Gemini-2.5-Flash as the backbone for both the Proposer and Fusor, and employed Gemini-Embedding (Lee et al., 2025) as the retriever. The retriever used the Korean component of the input document as the query for the Proposer, while utilizing both the input Hanja and the English translation drafts as the query for the Fusor. We employed 64 and 12 few-shot examples for the Proposer and the Fusor, respectively. During pseudo-labeling, the Fusor synthesized the final translation from five drafts generated by the Proposer with temperature of 0.3. Finally, to construct the pseudo-labeled dataset Daug, we applied the proposed augmentation strategy to 317.4K Hanja-Korean pairs from corpora not yet translated into English (excluding data from the King Sejong era), incurring cost of about $3,000. This augmented dataset is utilized to mitigate data sparsity and prevent potential overfitting toward specific historical period.

sections.title: Untranslated Corpus
sections.content: We present our model, Hanja-to-English historical document translation model fine-tuned on Qwen3 32B. Our model performs end-to-end translation from Hanja to English. Our training utilizes two datasets: pseudo-labeled dataset Daug and human-translated dataset Dtrain. We employ twostage training strategy: the first stage uses Daug to learn Hanja semantics and phonetic patterns of proper nouns, while the second stage leverages Dtrain to align the model with human-level stylistic nuances. The entire training process was executed on eight H200 GPUs, taking 15.1 hours for the first stage and 1.2 hours for the second stage. Finally, we deployed our model to translate all remaining untranslated AJD and JRS documents. Using eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the translation of these 2.09 million documents was completed in 94.6 hours, which is significantly faster and more cost effective than manual translation. To facilitate global accessibility to these historical records, both the dataset and the model are made publicly available.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Results
sections.content: In this section, we investigate optimal pseudolabeling settings and demonstrate our models superior performance against baselines including LLMbased and human expert evaluations.

sections.title: 5.1 Ablation of the Pseudo-Labeling Pipeline
sections.content: To comprehensively validate the effectiveness of glossary integration, input augmentation, and fewshot prompting strategies, we evaluated translation performance on Dtest using Gemini-2.5-Flash. All experimental results with costs on Batch API are summarized in Table 3. First, we observe significant improvement in translation performance when glossary is incorporated. This suggests that the glossary information facilitates better understanding of Hanja terms, aiding in their translation into appropriate English pronunciations. Similarly, providing pre-translated Korean inputs alongside the Hanja source text enhances the understanding of the input documents, indicating that Korean translations effectively support the pseudo-labeling process. The latter part of the table presents the impact of RAG and FusioN, and the input language on the retriever. Including few-shot examples yields substantial performance gains. In particular, while static shots also improve performance, examples that are relevant to the input document lead to much larger gains, highlighting the effectiveness of RAGbased methods for enhancing performance. For dynamic shots, using the Korean translation of the input Hanja as the retriever query resulted in better performance than using the Hanja input alone. This is because the embedding model used for retrieval was trained on larger corpus of Korean text compared to Hanja, resulting in superior comprehension of Korean.

Furthermore, we fine-tuned an additional Qwen3-32Bbased pivot translation baseline (Pivot-MT) under the same settings as our model. This baseline first translates Hanja into Korean and then translates the resulting Korean text into English. HERIT outperforms the Pivot-MT baseline, indicating that direct Hanja-to-English translation is more effective than pivot-based translation by avoiding error propagation across the two translation stages. To examine whether pseudo-labeling can eliminate the need for inference-time retrieval, we finetuned Qwen3-32B on Dtrain with glossary and RAG applied during both training and inference. Although this configuration outperforms the Dtrainonly baseline, it still falls short of HERIT. More critically, retrieval augmentation incurs substantial computational overheadexpanding the context length to over 8K tokens (increasing the input prompt length by 13 to 14 times) and scaling training computational cost by 9 times. By contrast, HERIT effectively distills external knowledge directly into model parameters, achieving superior translation quality while remaining retrieval-free and highly efficient for large-scale historical text translation.

sections.title: 5.3 LLM-Based and Human Evaluations
sections.content: Although Dtest consists of human-translated data, it is restricted to specific reign periods, which limits generalization across the entire chronological scope of the AJD corpus. To address this, we performed an LLM-based evaluation on the held-out dataset Dtest NT by sampling 80 documents from each of the remaining reign periods excluded from pseudolabeling. Adopting the method proposed by Zheng et al. (2023), models first generate translations for Dtest NT . Subsequently, the LLM Evaluator assesses the translation quality score on scale of 1 to 10, taking the source Hanja text and the modelgenerated English translation as inputs. To enhance score of 3.93, outperforming the baseline score of 3.22. In addition, HERIT achieved selection rate of 66.84% in the pairwise preference evaluation, which is more than twice that of the baseline. These results demonstrate the superior translation quality of HERIT in human expert evaluation.

sections.title: 6 Analysis
sections.content: This section evaluates the models robustness against temporal overfitting and provides qualitative analysis of translation examples. 6.1 Temporal Overfitting To investigate whether our method effectively mitigates temporal overfitting, we analyzed the human evaluation results. Since the evaluation samples were stratified by king, as detailed in Section 5.3, we computed the average score for each reign across both HERIT and the baseline, Qwen3 32B trained exclusively on human-labeled data. We then determined the performance gap between the two models for each reign and visualized these gaps chronologically. As noted in Section 2, the human-labeled corpus is heavily concentrated on documents from the reign of King Sejong. Consequently, Qwen3 trained on this temporally biased dataset performs comparably to HERIT during this specific period, as shown in Fig. 4. In contrast, HERIT consistently achieves superior performance on documents from other reigns. This indicates that training on data concentrated in single historical period leads to temporal overfitting, while the proposed pseudolabeling strategy helps mitigate this bias and enhances overall translation robustness.

sections.title: 6.2 Qualitative Analysis of Translations
sections.content: We also conducted qualitative comparison of HERIT against two baselines using samples from the test set: Qwen3 32B fine-tuned exclusively on human-translated data and Hunyuan-MT-7B, leading Chinese translation model. As shown in the first example in Table 6, both Qwen3 32B and HERIT correctly transliterated the proper nouns according to Korean pronunciation rules, whereas Hunyuan-MT-7B incorrectly relied on Chinese phonetics. In the second case, the term 房子 carries distinct semantics depending on the context: it denotes house in standard Chinese but refers to female palace servant in the context of the Joseon Dynasty. While Hunyuan-MT-7B Figure 3: Human expert evaluation scores and preference ratios for our model versus the baseline. the reliability of model-based evaluation, we provided the LLM Evaluator with the corresponding human-translated Korean text and glossary information as reference materials. We chose Sonnet-4.6 as the evaluator to avoid potential bias arising from the training process. As shown in Table 5, the LLM-based evaluation demonstrates that for both the 8B and 32B models, the two-stage learning approach combining pseudo-labeled and human-translated data outperforms models trained exclusively on humantranslated data. Notably, given that Dtest NT covers the entire AJD period disjoint from the training dataset, these results confirm the effectiveness of pseudolabeling in enhancing generalization. Furthermore, while incorporating the glossary and RAG into both training and inference slightly improves performance over the baseline trained solely on Dtrain, the two-stage model trained on Daug substantially outperforms the model finetuned with the glossary and RAG. This highlights that pseudo-labeling provides significant additional performance gains, demonstrating that our approach effectively generalizes across the entire AJD period rather than temporal overfitting to the specific timeframe of Dtrain. Additionally, using 200 examples sampled uniformly across different kings from Dtest NT , we recruited domain experts in Sinographic literature and Korean history who are proficient in English to evaluate our model against the baseline (Qwen3 32B trained solely on Dtrain). We asked the experts to rate each translation on scale of 1-5. Further, to differentiate between models in cases where scores were tied (excluding identical translations), we performed comparative evaluation where experts were instructed to select the better response. These results demonstrate HERITs superior ability to deliver precise translations by capturing both Sino-Korean lexical nuances and the unique contexts of historical documents.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In this study, we presented HERIT, systematic domain-adaptation pipeline designed to address the scarcity of parallel corpora in historical translation. By leveraging abundant intermediate resources through RAGand Fusion-based strategy, we developed robust method for generating highquality pseudo-labels without relying on costly human annotation. Extensive experiments, including both human and LLM-based evaluations, demonstrated that HERIT not only outperforms strong baselines but also effectively alleviates temporal overfitting, persistent challenge in analyzing historical archives. Furthermore, our results highlight the potential of LLM-based data augmentation for other low-resource classical languages where direct translation pairs are limited. By enabling the translation of previously inaccessible documents, our work facilitates broader access to historical archives, empowering researchers worldwide to engage more deeply with historical texts.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Due to budgetary constraints, we primarily employed Gemini-2.5-Flash for the Proposer and Fusor components, focusing exclusively on AJD documents for pseudo-labeling. We anticipate that employing more diverse set of LLMs as Proposers to enhance translation diversity, as well as incorporating JRS documents as targets, would yield higher-quality pseudo-labels. Furthermore, hardware limitations necessitated restricting the maximum sequence length to 2,048 tokens, with limit of 800 Hanja characters. Consequently, approximately 6.7% of the training data was filtered out. For inference, documents exceeding this limit were processed using chunking strategy. We expect that extending the models maximum input length will further improve translation performance.

sections.title: A Deduplication
sections.content: To justify our similarity threshold, Table 7 presents qualitative comparisons around the threshold. In Example 1, the sentence essentially repeats standardized tribute record with near-identical phrasing and semantics, justifying its removal. Conversely, Example 2 demonstrates why lower threshold would over-filter; replacing the ritual name (端 午 vs. 中秋) radically shifts the historical context, date, and English translation despite high lexical overlap. Manual inspection across intervals confirmed that 0.9 strictly eliminates near-duplicate administrative phrasing while preserving semantically distinct formulaic records. Figure 5 shows the distribution of maximum Levenshtein similarity between Dtest and Dtrain. The majority of evaluation samples (75.6%) exhibit low overlap ( 0.6). Crucially, no significant clustering is observed near the 0.90 boundary, ensuring that the benchmark remains well-isolated from training data and genuinely assesses generalization rather than template recall.

sections.title: B Training Details
sections.content: We trained the models for one epoch in each stage. To mitigate overfitting and prevent bias toward the later stage, we employed stage-specific learning rates. For the 32B model, the learning rates were set to 1 105 for the first stage and 5 106 for the second; for the 8B model, we applied 2 105 and 1 105, respectively. The batch size was set to 64 for the first stage and 16 for the second stage. All models were trained with the PagedAdamW 8-bit optimizer (Dettmers et al., 2022) and FSDP (Zhao et al., 2023) on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Figure 6: Performance and cost of the Proposer and Fusor across different numbers of few-shot examples.

sections.title: C Experimental Results
sections.content: C.1 Number of Few-shot Examples Fig. 6 illustrates the impact of the number of fewshot examples on the performance of both the Proposer and Fusor. Notably, the Proposer exhibits consistent performance gains up to 128 examples. However, to balance performance against the increased LLM inference costs incurred by larger shot sizes, we adopted 64-shot configuration for the Proposer during pseudo-labeling. Additionally, we identified that temperature of 0.3 and draft count of 5 provided the best performance, and thus utilized these parameters for pseudo-labeling. In contrast, although the Fusor also improves with more examples, its marginal gains are less pronounced than those of the Proposer. Therefore, considering the performance-cost trade-off, we set the few-shot size for the Fusor to 12. C.

In addition, we investigated the impact of proposer diversity on cost-effectiveness. The singleproposer setting relied solely on Gemini-2.5-Flash, whereas the diverse-proposer setting combined Qwen3 235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Sonnet 4.5. The results show that the single-model configuration achieves both better performance and higher cost efficiency. This suggests that while increasing model diversity yields wider variety of candidates, it does not necessarily translate into better performance, making the single-model configuration more cost-effective choice. To qualitatively verify that FusioN effectively synthesizes proposer-generated translations during the aggregation stage, we analyze the representative examples shown in Table 10. In the first example, while candidate (2) misinterprets the syntactic structure, yielding flawed translation, FusioN successfully adopts the correct phrasing from candidate (1), preserving semantic accuracy. In the second example, candidate (2) suffers from incomplete generation. FusioN effectively filters out this noise and consolidates valid information from the viable candidates to produce fluent and comprehensive translation. In the third example, although multiple candidates generate the generic term white falcon, FusioN selects the historically accurate term white goshawk provided by minority candidate, demonstrating its capability for fine-grained lexical selection. Overall, these cases illustrate that FusioN effectively aggregates candidate translations to ensure both factual correctness and grammatical fluency. sections.title: D Human Evaluation
sections.content: To compare our model against the baseline, we recruited three professional experts in Sinographic literature and Korean history who are proficient in English to evaluate 200 items. The evaluation was conducted in strict double-blind manner, ensuring that the evaluators remained completely unaware of the identity of the generating models. Prior to the task, the experts were provided with comprehensive instructions regarding the interface and the evaluation rubric. In addition, we developed custom web-based interface to facilitate this evaluation, as shown in Fig. 7. The interface displays the source Hanja text and the associated glossary at the top, while the anonymized outputs from both models are presented in the center. Evaluators rated each translation on 1-5 Likert scale. To ensure rigorous comparative analysis, forced-choice mechanism was implemented; whenever tie occurred (i.e., identical scores were given to both models), evaluators were required to select the superior translation based on three core criteria: Semantic coherence: The degree of preservation of the original meaning without omission the Proposer and Fusor prompts incorporate Korean translations provided by human experts, which serve as guidance for translating historical documents. The Fusor prompt largely follows the structure of the Proposer prompt, but differs in several key respects. Following the implementation of Khairi et al. (2025), it includes Task section describing the draft-fusion method and Fusion Steps section outlining the procedure. In the user prompt, the task instructions and guidelines from the Proposer stage are included under Translation Instruction, while the drafts generated by the Proposer are listed under Translation Candidates. The Fusor leverages these translation candidates to generate the final translation.
